title: THE CRY THAT SHOOK ETERNITY
paragraphs: THE CRY THAT SHOOK ETERNITY
The Meaning of “My God, Why Have You Forsaken Me?”
The sky turned black in the middle of the day.

Not at midnight.
Not during a storm.
Not after the crucifixion.
While He was still hanging there.

Blood-covered.
Mocked.
Abandoned by friends.
Rejected by religious leaders.
Surrounded by enemies.
And then came a cry so haunting that nearly two thousand years later humanity still struggles to comprehend it.
“Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?”
Matthew records the words in their original form:
“Ἠλί Ἠλί λεμὰ σαβαχθανί?” (Matthew 27:46)
Translated:
“My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
Many have read those words and concluded that Jesus lost faith.
Others assume He was overwhelmed by despair.
Some even suggest that God abandoned His Son.
But the deeper we go into Scripture, the more astonishing this moment becomes.
This was not the cry of a defeated Savior.
It was the cry of the victorious Lamb carrying the full weight of humanity's sin.
And hidden within these words is one of the greatest revelations of grace ever spoken.
To understand the cross, we must first understand the cry.
The words Jesus spoke were not random.
They were the opening line of Psalm 22.
In Hebrew:
אֵלִי אֵלִי לָמָה עֲזַבְתָּנִי
Eli, Eli, lama azavtani.
“My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
Jesus was quoting Scripture.
In Jewish culture, citing the first line of a Psalm often directed listeners to the entire Psalm.
What makes Psalm 22 extraordinary is that it was written approximately one thousand years before Christ's crucifixion.
Yet it describes details that sound as though someone stood beneath the cross and documented what they witnessed.
“They pierce my hands and feet.” (Psalm 22:16)
“They divide my garments among them and cast lots for my clothing.” (Psalm 22:18)
The Roman soldiers literally did exactly that.
The suffering of Christ was not an accident.
It was foretold.
Planned.
Promised.
The cross was not God losing control.
The cross was God fulfilling redemption.
But the question remains.
What did Jesus mean when He cried out those words?
Was He truly abandoned?
The answer requires us to stand on holy ground.
Scripture teaches that Jesus was completely sinless.
“He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in His mouth.” (1 Peter 2:22)
He lived the life humanity failed to live.
He obeyed where Adam rebelled.
He remained faithful where Israel wandered.
He stood righteous where every human being had fallen.
Yet on the cross something unprecedented happened.
Paul writes:
The Greek text of 2 Corinthians 5:21 is breathtaking:
τὸν μὴ γνόντα ἁμαρτίαν
“The One who knew no sin.”
Jesus did not become sinful.
He remained holy.
Yet He became the sin-bearer.
Every act of rebellion.
Every lie.
Every betrayal.
Every hidden addiction.
Every secret shame.
Every scandal.
Every act of violence.
Every moment of pride.
Every generation's accumulated guilt.
Placed upon Him.
Isaiah saw this centuries earlier.
“The LORD has laid on Him the iniquity of us all.” (Isaiah 53:6)
Imagine standing beneath an avalanche.
Now multiply that weight by every sin ever committed throughout human history.
The crushing burden that fell upon Christ cannot be measured.
This is where many theologians carefully explain that Jesus experienced the judgment our sins deserved.
Not because He was guilty.
But because He willingly stood in the place of the guilty.
The innocent One received the punishment of the guilty so the guilty could receive the righteousness of the innocent.
This is the heart of the Gospel.
Substitution.
Redemption.
Grace.
Yet something remarkable is often overlooked.
When Jesus quotes Psalm 22, He begins with anguish.
But Psalm 22 does not end in anguish.
Far from it.
The Psalm moves from suffering to victory.
From abandonment to vindication.
From darkness to worship.
From pain to triumph.
Near the end of Psalm 22 we read:
“He has not despised or abhorred the affliction of the afflicted, and He has not hidden His face from him.”
That changes everything.
The Psalm itself reveals that abandonment is not the final word.
God's presence remains.
God's purpose remains.
God's plan remains.
The darkness is real.
But so is the coming victory.
What looked like defeat was actually redemption unfolding before the eyes of the world.
Jesus was not merely expressing pain.
He was revealing prophecy.
He was declaring fulfillment.
He was pointing listeners to a Psalm that begins with suffering but ends with global worship.
The final verses envision nations turning to God.
Future generations proclaiming His righteousness.
People not yet born hearing about what God has done.
In many ways, Psalm 22 anticipates the spread of the Gospel itself.
The cry from the cross was never the end of the story.
It was the doorway to the resurrection.
And perhaps that is why this moment reaches so deeply into our own lives.
Because many people know what Psalm 22 feels like.
Not intellectually.
Personally.
The hospital room.
The funeral.
The divorce papers.
The addiction battle.
The unanswered prayer.
The betrayal by someone trusted.
The crushing loneliness.
The night when heaven seems silent.
The season when God feels distant.
Countless believers have whispered some version of the same question.
“God, where are You?”
Yet Scripture repeatedly teaches that feelings are not always reality.
Jesus felt the horror of bearing sin's judgment.
But the Father had not abandoned His redemptive plan.
Likewise, believers often walk through valleys where God's presence feels hidden.
Yet His promises remain unchanged.
David wrote:
“Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for You are with me.”
Notice the wording.
Not around the valley.
Not over the valley.
Through the valley.
The Gospel does not promise the absence of suffering.
It promises the presence of Christ within suffering.
The cross proves that God understands pain from the inside.
He is not distant from human suffering.
He entered it.
He carried it.
He conquered it.
This is why the cry of Jesus is ultimately not a message of despair.
It is a message of hope.
Because the One who cried, “Why have You forsaken Me?” also cried, “It is finished.”
In Greek:
Τετέλεσται
Tetelestai.
A commercial term meaning:
“Paid in full.”
The debt was canceled.
The ransom was completed.
The work was accomplished.
Sin's claim was broken.
Death's authority was shattered.
Hell's victory was reversed.
Three days later the tomb would stand empty.
The cry of abandonment would give way to the declaration of resurrection.
And that changes everything.
The scandal of humanity met the grace of God at the cross.
Every failure.
Every secret.
Every regret.
Every stain.
Every shattered story.
Every broken life.
All of it collided with divine mercy.
The cross is where scandal meets grace.
It is where rebels become sons and daughters.
It is where the guilty are declared righteous.
It is where the condemned find forgiveness.
It is where the hopeless discover hope.
It is where sinners meet a Savior who refused to leave them where they were.
The greatest scandal in history was not that humanity crucified the Son of God.
The greater scandal is that the Son of God willingly died for the very people crucifying Him.
And because He did, no story is beyond redemption.
No life is beyond restoration.
No past is beyond forgiveness.
No sinner is beyond the reach of grace.
When Jesus cried, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” He entered the deepest darkness so that those who trust Him would never have to face eternal separation from God.
He walked into judgment so believers could walk into mercy.
He endured wrath so sinners could receive grace.
He embraced the cross so that broken people could receive a new name, a new heart, and a new future.
Perhaps that is why these words continue to echo across centuries.
Because somewhere beneath the theology is a deeply personal truth.
Every believer eventually discovers that the cross is not merely something Jesus did.
It is something Jesus did for them.
And once that reality reaches the heart, everything changes.

Comment what stood out most to you from Christ's cry on the cross. Was there a season when God felt distant, only for you to later discover He was working in ways you could not see? Your testimony may become someone else's encouragement.
The darkest cry in history became the brightest invitation ever given.
